rows.title: The collapse of two well-funded heavyweights in Colorado’s outdoor recreation realm
rows.standfirst: Future Legends, the struggling developer of an 118-acre sports complex in Windsor files for bankruptcy amid lawsuits from angry contractors and used bike seller The Pro’s Closet closes shop after 18 years and nearly $100 million in funding

rows.title: What’s Working: Colorado still searching for cause of labor data that shows state lost 72,700 jobs in Q1
rows.standfirst: A technology update to the unemployment system is the likely culprit, says the state labor department, but cause not yet determined. Plus: Job openings flat, air travel slows and more!

rows.title: Is a Supreme Court fight over 88-mile Uinta Basin Railway really a battle over NEPA?
rows.standfirst: Dozens of industry groups, lawmakers, local governments and environmental advocates have weighed in on the scope of the National Environmental Policy Act rather than 88 miles of new tracks that would link Utah oilfields to the national rail network

rows.title: Xcel Energy ordered to remove investor relations and executive salaries from costs passed on to Colorado consumers
rows.standfirst: Colorado regulators are putting into play a law passed in 2023 in response to a 52% hike in winter gas bills

rows.title: Colorado company is building its own WALL-E as it reimagines trash disposal, recycling in outer space
rows.standfirst: Sierra Space is building a trash compactor for the space station that’s similar to the Disney character, while others are working on detecting space debris to avoid big damages

rows.title: Clean-car sales jump 10% as Coloradans lean on state, federal and utility rebates
rows.standfirst: EVs, plug-in hybrids, and hybrids made up 38% of vehicle registrations in third quarter of 2024

rows.title: What’s Working: Colorado builders stick with rate incentives to attract new-home buyers
rows.standfirst: Mortgage rates are up from the summer, despite two federal interest rate cuts. Plus: Rental incentives, Colorado broadband awards and more!

rows.title: The TV peak for “American Ninja Warrior” has passed. But Colorado’s young stars are growing the sport off screen.
rows.standfirst: As the state becomes a hub for ninja competition, a generation of stars is making the progression from fan to competitor to entrepreneur

rows.title: Denver heat pump incentive targets multifamily, commercial buildings for more efficient heating and cooling
rows.standfirst: Stores, offices and apartment buildings are in line for $7.5 million in help to cut monthly energy bills by installing new systems

rows.title: Denver Ballot Issue 2R: Voters reject sales tax for affordable housing
rows.standfirst: The measure would have raised an estimated $100 million a year to address the city’s housing shortage

rows.title: Denver Broncos on verge of giving fans faster internet at Mile High stadium
rows.standfirst: Who uses mobile phones at football games? More Broncos fans than ever, as stadium upgrades wireless technology to help fans, staff and even Taylor Swift concertgoers.

rows.title: What’s Working: More than half of Denver-area homes sold last month offered a concession
rows.standfirst: Affordability is still an issue statewide. Colorado Springs agents report price reductions.

rows.title: A second Trump presidency could create big shifts in Colorado’s outdoor recreation economy
rows.standfirst: Could Trump fiddle with Biden’s Camp Hale and Thompson Divide mineral withdrawal? Will a return of tariffs and visa bans hurt recreation businesses? Will the BLM return to Grand Junction?

rows.title: Agriculture in Colorado under Trump’s presidency: Less conservation, more deregulation
rows.standfirst: Project 2025 outlines a plan to deprioritize climate-smart programs and put small farms at greater risk

rows.title: Colorado companies prepare for Trump’s promised tariffs. Who’ll end up bearing the cost is still a question.
rows.standfirst: Trump’s promise of 10% to 60% tariffs isn’t yet reality. But Colorado companies are talking about adjusting operations and inventories.

rows.title: Colorado, federal government could be at odds on oil and gas priorities under Trump’s presidency
rows.standfirst: The once and future president has promised to drill on federal lands. How would that affect already established legal settlements in the state?

rows.title: How Donald Trump’s presidency may impact 10 areas that Coloradans care about most
rows.standfirst: Vows to overhaul federal policies send powerful signals on immigration, the environment, health care and more.

rows.title: Denver’s convention industry is partying like it’s 2019
rows.standfirst: And 2025 is expected to be even busier, as outsider interest in visiting Denver returns. But some wonder, could recovery have been faster?

rows.title: Erie residents fend off Weld County oil wells that would have extended 5 miles under their town — for now
rows.standfirst: “Chess game” continues as state commission tells oil and gas company to go back and exhaust all other locations for the Draco pad

rows.title: Colorado marijuana sales — and tax dollars — are still falling. The rise of intoxicating hemp may be to blame.
rows.standfirst: Marijuana sales peaked in Colorado in the 2020-21 budget year, when the state collected $424 million in taxes. That fell to $248 million last year.

rows.title: Union at homeless youth nonprofit Urban Peak achieves elusive first contract
rows.standfirst: Employees of the Denver nonprofit, which provides shelter for homeless youth, get farther than local Starbucks workers and more than 100 other locals that have unionized since 2020.

rows.title: Xcel runs out of EV rebates in bad news/good news for Colorado culture and economic switch
rows.standfirst: Some customers are stuck without checks, but dealers are happy about the boost in electric vehicle sales

rows.title: What’s Working: Colorado’s job growth ahead of US but unemployment rate rises to 4.1%
rows.standfirst: The state is tops for job creation but for less obvious reasons. Plus: A national quarterly jobs report suspends Colorado due to “data quality” issues, our fastest-growing companies, more!

rows.title: How much water do Colorado communities actually need? In one, surprisingly little.
rows.standfirst: With new houses using 30% less water, Sterling Ranch asked Douglas County for tighter household limits. That’s a far cry from traditional planning where cities routinely ask for more water.

rows.title: Colorado’s Thanksgiving dinner cost is the 4th-highest in the country, even as prices nationwide drop
rows.standfirst: Turkey prices are down but a contributing factor is changing consumer tastes rather than inflation. Plus: The most congested travel days this Thanksgiving in Colorado

rows.title: Will cage-free eggs be required in Colorado starting in 2025?
rows.standfirst: A state law is bringing new requirements for any Colorado egg-producer with more than 3,000 egg-laying hens

rows.title: Jared Polis is headed for another showdown with Democrats at the Colorado Capitol over union issues
rows.standfirst: The governor quickly pooh-poohed the bill Colorado’s labor movement says will be their priority in the legislature next year. That comes after he vetoed three union bills passed by the General Assembly in 2024.

rows.title: Did Colorado’s cage-free law cause an egg shortage?
rows.standfirst: Starting Jan. 1, all eggs sold in Colorado must be from cage-free chickens

rows.title: Colorado finally makes a scrap of progress on recycling goals after years of stagnation
rows.standfirst: Advocates say more big changes ahead in stymied efforts to divert waste from landfills

rows.title: Developers have the go-ahead for new construction in northern Weld County after a three-year freeze
rows.standfirst: Facing an onslaught of development proposals, a local water district pressed pause — hard. Now, the district is confident it can once again review requests for new water services.

rows.title: Residents rally to buy mobile home park and protect affordable housing in Lafayette
rows.standfirst: Now a resident-owned community, La Luna Community Cooperative dipped into a unique funding pool to make the $4.5 million purchase
